nameStory: The Decorated Mop gets its charming name from its fluffy, ornate appearance that resembles a fancy feather duster or decorative mop. Some folks also call it "prunes and custard" because of its rich purplish-brown and creamy yellow colors that look just like that classic dessert combination.
description: The Decorated Mop is a medium-sized mushroom with a beautifully colored cap that shows off rich purple-brown and golden-yellow tones. It typically grows 2-4 inches across the cap and has closely spaced gills underneath. This eye-catching fungus has a sturdy stem and grows in small clusters or groups. Its striking color combination makes it one of the more photogenic mushrooms you'll encounter in New England woods.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Rich purple-brown center fading to golden-yellow edges, with a slightly sticky feel when moist and a decorative, almost fuzzy appearance

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Creamy yellow to pale golden color, closely spaced and attached to the stem, with a soft, delicate texture

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Yellow to golden-brown, often with darker purple-brown fibers or scales, solid and firm to the touch

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: White spore print when collected on paper overnight

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Pleasant, mild mushroomy scent without any strong or unpleasant odors

habitat: Found growing on decaying hardwood logs and stumps throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. Look for it especially on rotting oak, maple, and beech wood in moist, shaded areas. It prefers well-established forest floors with plenty of woody debris rather than disturbed or open areas.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in spring, though occasional early specimens may appear in late May during warm, wet periods.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season begins in mid to late summer, especially after periods of rain when the forest floor stays consistently moist.
seasonality.fall: Most abundant in early to mid-fall when cool temperatures and autumn rains create ideal conditions for fruiting on decaying logs.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent during winter months as cold temperatures halt all fungal activity.

funFact: The Decorated Mop can actually help determine the health of a forest ecosystem because it only grows on wood that's in just the right stage of decay—not too fresh and not too far gone—making it a living indicator of balanced decomposition cycles.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its close relative Plums-and-Custard, but the Decorated Mop has more distinct purple-brown coloring concentrated in the cap center, while Plums-and-Custard shows more reddish tones throughout. Memory trick: "Decorated" has more contrast between its dark center and light edges.
contextualKnowledge: Despite having two different common names (Decorated Mop and prunes and custard), this is the exact same species—the naming difference comes from different regional traditions and whether people focus on its texture or color pattern.
compareHints: Among its Tricholomopsis relatives, Decorated Mop stands out with its distinctive purple-brown and yellow color pattern. Plums-and-Custard tends toward more reddish hues overall, while other species in the genus typically show more uniform yellow, orange, or brown coloring without the dramatic two-toned effect. The Decorated Mop's color contrast is its signature feature within this group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Plums-and-custard stands out among its Tricholomopsis relatives primarily due to its distinctive reddish-purple coloration and preference for coniferous wood.
